title: Smallest Range II
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Every element must be shifted by exactly `k`: each `nums[i]` is replaced by either `nums[i] + k` or `nums[i] - k`, and you choose the direction separately for each index.

After all the shifts, the score is the largest element minus the smallest element. Return the lowest score you can reach.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying both directions for every element is 2^n choices. Sorting reveals the structure: in some optimal answer, the smaller values all move up and the larger values all move down. If a smaller value went down while a larger one went up, swapping their directions could only pull the extremes closer together. So after sorting there is a split point `i`: indices `0..i` get `+k` and indices `i+1..n-1` get `-k`. Only `n - 1` splits (plus "all the same direction") need checking.

## Approach

1. Sort `nums` ascending.
2. Set `best` to `nums[n - 1] - nums[0]`: shifting every element the same way keeps the original spread.
3. For each split `i` from `0` to `n - 2`, the left part `0..i` goes up and the right part goes down.
4. The new maximum `high` is either the top of the left part (`nums[i] + k`) or the top of the right part (`nums[n - 1] - k`).
5. The new minimum `low` is either the bottom of the left part (`nums[0] + k`) or the bottom of the right part (`nums[i + 1] - k`).
6. Keep the smallest `high - low` in `best` and return it.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1]`, `k = 0`. After sorting, `n = 1` and `best = 1 - 1 = 0`. There is no split to try (the loop runs while `i < 0`), so the answer is `0`.

For a richer case, Example 3 sorts to `[1, 3, 6]` with `k = 3` and `best = 5`. Split `i = 0`: `high = max(4, 3) = 4`, `low = min(4, 0) = 0`, giving 4. Split `i = 1`: `high = max(6, 3) = 6`, `low = min(4, 3) = 3`, giving 3. The answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): the sort dominates; the scan over splits is O(n).
- Space: O(1) beyond the sort.

## Pitfalls

- Do not forget the "no split" case: `best` must start at the original spread, or a single element (or `k` larger than the spread) gives a wrong answer.
- `high` and `low` each have two candidates; using only `nums[n - 1] - k` or only `nums[0] + k` misses cases where the split boundary sets the extreme.
- Values may become negative after subtracting `k`; that is allowed and needs no clamping.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `best` | smallest score found so far |
| `i` | last index of the part shifted up |
| `high` | largest value after this split |
| `low` | smallest value after this split |

narration.2: Sort so that an optimal choice is a prefix moving up and a suffix moving down.
narration.4: Moving every element the same way keeps the original spread, a valid starting answer.
narration.6: Try each split point i: indices 0..i go up by k, the rest go down by k.
narration.7: The largest value is the top of the raised prefix or the top of the lowered suffix.
narration.8: The smallest value is the bottom of the raised prefix or the bottom of the lowered suffix.
narration.9: Keep the smallest score among all splits.
narration.11: Every split has been tried; return the best score.
